reason: §58 calls 'the king-priest Melchizedek' 'a figure of Christ' in so many words. The text names Christ, not only his priesthood, and 'king-priest' covers both offices, so `christ` is the right precision beside the existing melchizedek → christ-high-priest (§1544).
§60 says the chosen people were 'called to prepare for that day when God would gather all his children into the unity of the Church': preparatory wording about the people itself. Ecclesial is right.

§62 gives the Law's purpose, 'so that they would look for the promised Savior', which presents the Law as preparing Israel for Christ (cf. Gal 3:24). It is the weakest acceptable form of preparatory (a purpose clause, not 'prepared'/'fulfilled'), but the link is in the text.

§64 sets Mary as 'the purest figure among' the holy women who kept Israel's hope alive. 'Figure' here means a person among them, not a type, so teaches-only is right; the named women's Types (sarah, miriam, deborah, hannah, judith, esther) could also take a TEACHES edge from §64.

§65 is about the completeness of revelation in the Son; the prophets appear only inside the Heb 1:1 quotation as earlier speakers of God's word 'in parts'. That is prophetic speech contrasted with the one Word, not the prophets as figures of Christ, so a TEACHES edge to `the-prophets` overreaches.
§117 says verbatim that 'the crossing of the Red Sea is a sign or type ... of Christian Baptism'. Explicit, Sacramental, and the pair already exists.
The same sentence of §117 calls the crossing 'a sign or type of Christ's victory'. Explicit and Christological.

§122 teaches that the OT economy was 'deliberately so oriented that it should prepare for ... the coming of Christ' and that the mystery of salvation is 'present in a hidden way' in it. This is the ground of typology, the same kind of general statement as §§128-130, which already TEACH christ.
§128 defines typology as discerning 'prefigurations of what he accomplished ... in the person of his incarnate Son'. Already in the seed; TEACHES christ is right.
§129 tells Christians to read the OT 'in the light of Christ crucified and risen' and calls this 'typological reading'. Already in the seed; correct.
§130 uses 'the exodus from Egypt' as its own example of a typological 'intermediate stage' that keeps its value in God's plan, so the paragraph really teaches about that Type.

§204 is about the burning-bush theophany as the revelation 'fundamental ... for both the Old and the New Covenants', so it teaches about the Type. Caveat: what it teaches is the revealing of the Name, not the bush as a figure, so §204 should not be cited as a source for burning-bush → christ.

§280 calls creation the 'beginning of the history of salvation that culminates in Christ' and says 'from the beginning, God envisaged the glory of the new creation in Christ': fulfilment language, so preparatory and Christological hold. The 'culminates in Christ' clause carries the link better than the chosen quote.

§281 explains that the Easter Vigil, 'the celebration of the new creation in Christ', opens with the creation account: the liturgy reads creation toward its fulfilment. TEACHES the creation Type is right.

§312 sets Joseph's 'God meant it for good' beside 'the rejection and murder of God's only Son', from which God brought our redemption; this bears directly on joseph → christ. The text does not call Joseph a figure, so teaches-only is the right label.

§314's 'that definitive sabbath rest for which he created heaven and earth' names creation's final end in sabbath terms, and 'definitive' implies the provisional seventh-day rest it completes (cf. Heb 4:9-10). The link is real but thin, since the OT Sabbath is implied rather than named; preparatory and Eschatological are the right labels.

§315 calls creation 'the first proclamation of the plan of his loving goodness, which finds its goal in the new creation in Christ'. Grammatically the goal belongs to the plan, but creation is the plan's first act, so 'finds its goal in' is fulfilment wording and preparatory holds.

§349, 'The first creation finds its meaning and its summit in the new creation in Christ', is the clearest fulfilment statement of the three. It is preparatory, not explicit (no figure wording); Christological fits the eighth day of the Resurrection.

§349 teaches that 'the seventh day completes the first creation' while the eighth day, the Resurrection, begins the new; it treats the Sabbath substantively. Teaches-only is right because the two days are set in sequence, not as figure and fulfilment.

Chrysologus, quoted in §359, says 'the second Adam stamped his image on the first Adam' and 'took on himself the role and the name of the first Adam'. That is image wording that makes Adam the copy of Christ (cf. Rom 5:14), so explicit holds here, unlike §411.
§374 measures the first man's original state against 'the glory of the new creation in Christ', which alone surpasses it. It teaches about Adam in his relation to Christ.
§388: 'We must know Christ as the source of grace in order to know Adam as the source of sin.' The Adam–Christ parallel is the point of the paragraph.
§402 cites Rom 5:18-19, setting one man's trespass against one man's righteousness. It teaches the Pauline Adam–Christ contrast without figure wording, so teaches-only is right.

'The Christian tradition sees in this passage an announcement' refers to the Gen 3:15 oracle, which is prophecy; the Adam → Christ link itself rests only on the title 'New Adam' and the obedience/disobedience contrast, with no figure/type/image wording. At most preparatory (the explicit support for this pair is §359).

§433 moves from the mercy seat as 'the place of God's presence' to Christ's humanity, in which 'God was in Christ reconciling', by way of Paul's 'expiation' (hilasterion, Rom 3:25, the mercy seat's own name in Heb 9:5). The link is in the text, though the Greek carries it; preparatory is the closest label and `christ` the right antitype.

§436 argues from the anointing of kings, priests and prophets to the Messiah anointed 'at once as king and priest, and also as prophet', and says Jesus 'fulfilled the messianic hope of Israel in his threefold office'. Preparatory and Christological are right.

§489 says the mission of many holy women 'prepared for that of Mary' and names Deborah among them. Preparatory and Marian are exact. Add the opening sentence ('the mission of many holy women *prepared* for that of Mary') to the quote, since that sentence carries the label.

§489 names Esther among the holy women whose mission 'prepared for that of Mary'. Preparatory and Marian are exact. Add the opening sentence ('the mission of many holy women *prepared* for that of Mary') to the quote, since that sentence carries the label.
§489 names Eve first, with the promise of a victorious posterity and of being 'mother of all the living', under the governing 'prepared for that of Mary'. Preparatory and Marian are exact.

§489 names 'Hannah, the mother of Samuel' among the holy women whose mission 'prepared for that of Mary'. Preparatory and Marian are exact. Add the opening sentence ('the mission of many holy women *prepared* for that of Mary') to the quote, since that sentence carries the label.

§489 names Ruth among the holy women whose mission 'prepared for that of Mary'. Preparatory and Marian are exact. Add the opening sentence ('the mission of many holy women *prepared* for that of Mary') to the quote, since that sentence carries the label.

The link is right: §489 says 'By virtue of this promise, Sarah conceives a son in spite of her old age' under the governing 'prepared for that of Mary'. But the quoted sentence never names Sarah; add that sentence to the quote.

§494 gives the Fathers' Eve–Mary antithesis ('The knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience') and transfers Eve's title 'Mother of the living' to Mary, but uses no figure/type/image/prefigure wording. The link is real but at most preparatory, as in §489.

Both existing links read true under 'Israel, the Chosen People': Israel as God's son read of Christ (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15), and the people called to prepare for the Church (§60). It is rightly kept distinct from `the-synagogue-old-covenant-assembly` and `the-faithful-remnant`, and the description keeps Jeshurun (Deut 32:15; Isa 44:2).

A real figure the Catechism needs ('the first creation', §§280, 315, 349), and the description is faithful to Gen 1:1-2:3. The merged §§759/778 rows ('from the beginning') should be judged on their own, since their sense may only be temporal.

A distinct NT reality the Catechism names repeatedly (2 Cor 5:17; Gal 6:15; Rev 21:5), and no existing NT Type covers it. Optional: the description could also name the believer made a new creature in Baptism, since 2 Cor 5:17 is personal (cf. §1265).

About private revelations and Christ as the fulfilment of Revelation; no OT figure.

'Types of historical writing' means literary genres, not typology.

'The Old Testament prepares for the New and the New Testament fulfills the Old' is a general statement with no concrete figure; at most a general TEACHES christ.
Abraham 'fulfills the definition of faith' in Heb 11:1 means he exemplifies it; there is no type and antitype.
